editorialNote: Scholarly study connections grounded in source texts. Labels distinguish exact wording, direct interpretation, parallels and counterpoints. The book-title allusion to Ezekiel is not an exegesis of Ezekiel.

entries.note: The year-chronogram 'צדקות אהב' is the actual language of this verse. It should be distinguished from the book-title allusion in Ezekiel.
The book title 'צדקת הצדיק' echoes these exact words. This is a title allusion, not a claim that the opening teaching expounds Ezekiel's discussion of responsibility.
Rav Tzadok describes the righteousness of the tzaddik as joining the three pillars into one encompassing foundation; a thematic exploration of the book's title, not an explicit citation of Ezekiel.
Explains the tzaddik as one whose distinguishing attribute includes guarding concrete actions, illustrating an aspect of practical righteousness rather than interpreting Ezekiel 18:20.
The command to eat the Korban Pesach 'בחפזון' is the Torah basis for Rav Tzadok's example of urgent beginnings.
The Mishnah explicitly contrasts Pesach Mitzrayim, eaten in haste, with Pesach Doros. This is the closest source for both halves of Rav Tzadok's comparison.
The Torah explains matzah through 'כי בחפזון יצאת מארץ מצרים'—the haste of the Exodus, alongside the haste of eating the original Pesach.
The prophetic future redemption is 'not in haste.' Compare Rav Tzadok's movement from urgent breakthrough to steady, mature progress.

entries.ref: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 2:3
entries.note: An especially close cross-reference: Rav Tzadok explicitly invokes Pesach Mitzrayim eaten hastily to distinguish the need to seize initial inspiration from later measured deliberation.
Explains why the original redemption and the matzah had to be hurried: a revelatory spiritual moment is transient and must be acted upon before it recedes; contrasts Isaiah 52:12.
The Exodus took place through spiritual leaping, rather than gradual ascent; the Korban Pesach blood expresses wholehearted dedication in the moment of breakthrough.
The urgency of leaving Egypt is discussed as necessary in the process of separation and redemption.
The readiness to eat Pesach with sandals and staff expresses Israel's immediate willingness to follow Hashem, even before the journey begins.

entries.kind: Pesach Mitzrayim versus Doros · Rav Tzadok
entries.note: Begins from the Mishnah's contrast between the Egyptian Pesach and subsequent observances, offering a further investigation of the distinction.
Expounds 'כי לא בחפזון תצאו' in Isaiah 52:12, supplying a counterpoint to the first redemption's necessary haste.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 25:1
entries.note: The abbreviated time for eating the Pesach is connected with acting swiftly upon a clearly recognized divine will and with redemption occurring in a leap.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 35:1
entries.note: Interprets the haste of eating matzah as an inner love that draws Israel after God's will before reflective deliberation.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 38:1
entries.note: Israel's haste in the Exodus is linked to the later readiness to say 'נעשה' before 'נשמע'—an eager capacity to accept divine service.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 42:2
entries.note: The swift eating of Pesach mirrors the divine gift of redemption as a sudden leap beyond ordinary stages.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 45:1
entries.note: Quotes the girded loins, sandals, staff, and hasty eating of Exodus 12:11; the first Pesach begins with an unearned burst of higher illumination.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 4:2
entries.note: Compares the haste of the Exodus with 'לא בחפזון תצאו' describing the future redemption's fuller, more integrated illumination.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 9:1
entries.kind: Divine initiative and human response · Ishbitz–Radzin
entries.note: Explains the initial salvation as coming beyond human grasp; the hurried departure calls for a corresponding human response.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 29:3
entries.note: Explains the first Pesach as a sudden gift while Israel was spiritually immature; eager running after God is later expressed in 'נעשה ונשמע'.

entries.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 1:2
entries.note: The original redemption came ahead of ordinary maturation, by spiritual skipping and haste.

entries.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:4
entries.note: Avraham's extraordinary alacrity is the ability to respond immediately when the will of Hashem is recognized, overcoming bodily inertia.

entries.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:5
entries.note: Avraham senses God's will 'כרגע' and moves without impediment, closely paralleling the instruction to seize the first spark of awakening.

entries.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:7
entries.note: Explains Yetziat Mitzrayim as release from entrenched desires and habits, so that a person can follow God's will at any moment.
Warns that uncalibrated zeal can overrun the proper spiritual stage; complements the opening instruction that haste must yield to restraint and measured progress.
